transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen, Daniel Ortiz, Priya Rao (Redwood); Alex Ward, Sana Mir, Jules Park, Tom Becker (Oxford Bridge)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming completions and sustained throughput. Oxford Bridge is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private VPC for a chat/notification product with spiky bursts (token storms) and stringent p95 SLOs (target 250ms-500ms for short responses, up to 1s for longer streaming). They care about concurrency, cold-starts, KV/prefix cache behavior, and audit/security controls.

Topics discussed:
- p95 latency targets by response length
- concurrency and burst sizing
- streaming vs batched throughput (tokens/sec)
- hosting decision tradeoffs (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
- security requirements (SAML, KMS, audit logs)
- next steps: traffic sample + benchmark run

Quick action items (as noted in call):
- see action_items field above for formal owners

Transcript (timestamps approximate, auto-generated - may contain transcription errors):
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): ok everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep to 45 minutes, quick intros then jump into the p95 targets you mentioned in the RFC, Alex?
[00:12] Alex (Oxford Bridge): yeah thanks, I'm Alex, eng lead, we're building the realtime assistant and we have a lot of small messages — most are 30 to 120 tokens but we get these big summarize flows occasionally, so p95 matters a lot for user experience.
[00:28] Daniel (Redwood): cool, do you have a current p95 today or a target you want to hit?
[00:33] Alex: current system is in-house, p95 for the short prompts sits around 800ms on average and spikes to 1.6s during bursts, we want to get under 500ms ideally for short ones and cap long streaming at about a second.
[00:46] Sana (Oxford Bridge): and we do care about streaming — incremental tokens show in product as they arrive, so tail latency is visible to users.
[00:54] Priya (Redwood): okay so we're talking streaming p95 and also concurrency. what's your expected concurrency at peak?
[01:02] Jules (Oxford Bridge): we had a recent spike test, about 1.2k concurrent users generating ~900 concurrent model streams, average tokens per stream ~60, but bursts can push to 3k streams for short windows.
[01:18] Tom (CTO): important note — data residency and audit logs matter for us, we need SAML SSO and KMS integration for keys.
[01:26] Maya: totally, we can cover both hosted and private with those controls; Dedicated also supports customer-managed KMS.
[01:34] Alex: walk us through how Redwood handles KV cache and prefix caching during streaming, because our summaries reuse context a lot and we want to avoid repeated compute.
[01:45] Daniel: sure, so our runtime exposes KV caching which holds attention key/value cache between calls when you pin sessions or there's a shared prefix, it reduces repeated decode work. in Hosted we do automatic prefix caching when routes are stable; for Dedicated/Private you can configure longer cache TTLs and pinning policies.
[02:03] Alex: hmm, does that apply across shards if we're running multi-GPU?
[02:07] Daniel: yes, the KV cache can be sharded but the runtime does cross-shard cache lookup, so warm cache hits still avoid recomputation. small caveat — there's a uniformity cost if your requests jump between model variants.
[02:19] Sana: and what about token/sec throughput numbers? we need to size for token/sec and tokens per second during bursts.
[02:27] Daniel: for a 7B-ish open model on A100 equivalent, in our tests baseline continuous throughput per GPU for streaming is about 2500-3500 tokens/sec for medium contexts, p95 depends on sequence length and concurrency and batching. but that's a rough ballpark, we'll run your profile against the harness.
[02:43] Alex: that number sounds promising — but we saw varying numbers from vendors, sometimes they quote peak single-thread token rates that don't reflect p95 under concurrency.
[02:53] Priya: yeah, that's a frequent pitfall. we'll show both steady-state tokens/sec and p95 for short/long responses in the benchmark report.
[03:05] Jules: what's your typical cold-start for a model variant or serving container? we want to know impact during scale-ups.
[03:11] Daniel: cold-start depends on model size and whether weights are resident; Hosted uses warm pools and prefetch for common variants — 200–600ms for small-medium models in many cases, long models obviously longer. Dedicated gives you pinned instances for predictable starts; Private lets you control pre-warming.
[03:27] Tom: we have tight budget constraints so we might prefer Hosted for lower ops overhead but worried about noisy neighbors and consistent p95.
[03:35] Maya: understood — tradeoff is cost predictability vs control. we typically recommend Dedicated for customers with predictable high concurrency or strict p95 SLOs; Hosted is great for rapid launch and many customers still meet 95th targets with autoscaling and routing policies.
[03:52] Alex: how do you do routing/fallbacks in case of overload? we need graceful degradation, e.g., drop to cheaper model or shorter length before failing.
[03:59] Priya: we support policy-level routing: route by latency, cost, or region; automatic fallback to a compatible quantized variant or shorter response policy. you can define canary rules and circuit-breaker thresholds.
[04:12] Alex: nice. we also have compliance check — can you provide SOC2/ISO docs and audit log sampling?
[04:18] Maya: yes, we'll send security docs; Hosted includes audit logs and retention settings, Dedicated/Private can integrate with your SIEM.
[04:26] Jules: in terms of benchmarking, what do you need from us to run a meaningful p95 run?
[04:30] Daniel: the most useful is a sample traffic CSV: timestamp, tokens requested, token per response distribution, concurrency histogram, and a small set of representative prompts including streaming prompts. also indicate which prompts are highest priority for p95.
[04:42] Jules: we can extract that from our metrics platform, we'll share by Friday.
[04:46] Maya: perfect. we'll then schedule a 60-minute run with SRE involved; we'll also include a short smoke on Redwood Hosted test tenant to show baseline numbers.
[04:58] Tom: timeline wise we're aiming for a decision in 3–4 weeks, proof-of-concept first then pilot.
[05:04] Maya: that's reasonable. any blockers from your side for private hosting?
[05:08] Sana: main blockers are audit/KMS and network — our infra team will want a VPC peering plan.
[05:14] Priya: we have docs on VPC peering and private control plane; we'll attach them.
[05:20] Alex: curious — do you have any published benchmarks comparing hosted vs dedicated for p95 under bursty traffic?
[05:26] Daniel: we have internal benchmark notes and a summary we share with prospects; it's not a one-size-fits-all number but we can provide example p95 curves per tokens/seq and concurrency.
[05:36] Alex: ok, a few nitty-gritty questions: are you doing quantized kernels and how do they affect streaming tail?
[05:43] Daniel: yes, we support quantized kernels; they reduce memory and can slightly increase per-token latency in some models but usually net positive for throughput. streaming tail can be fine as long as the kernels are optimized for attention patterns; we also support mixed precision.
[05:56] Jules: error handling — if a node OOMs during a burst, do you have fallback routing?
[06:01] Maya: yes, automatic fallback to spare capacity or to a lower-cost model variant; we also surface retries and circuit breakers in the console.
[06:10] Alex: for the benchmark, can you show both p95 and token/sec and also annotate the contribution from batching vs KV cache hits?
[06:17] Daniel: yup we will. we'll show breakdown: raw decode time per token, batching gains, cache hit delta, network egress time.
[06:25] Sana: one more — what's the overhead of server-side encryption/KMS on latency?
[06:29] Priya: KMS calls are async for model keys in most setups, negligible per-token, but initial key unwrap on a new container can add ~10–50ms, depends on HSM and topology.
[06:40] Tom: ok great.
[06:42] Maya: summary: Oxford Bridge to share traffic sample and security checklist; Redwood to run perf harness and share recommendation Hosted vs Dedicated with numbers; follow-up benchmark session to be scheduled.
[06:54] Alex: sounds good, thanks all.
[06:58] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and next steps after this.
[07:03] (End of recording)

Notes on transcription: some brand names and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., K-V cache, V-P-C), speaker labels auto-assigned; timestamps approximate.
